paras: The lynching of George White took place on the night of June 22-23, 1903, when a crowd of several thousand broke into the New Castle County workhouse near Wilmington, Delaware, and burned White, a Black man charged with killing Helen S. Bishop, at a stake in a nearby field. A boy in the attacking crowd was fatally shot, and in September a grand jury declined to indict anyone.

Bishop, a seventeen-year-old high school student, was attacked on her way home from school on June 15 and died the next day. White, a worker employed by Edward Woodward, was held in the county workhouse, and on June 18 the court refused a special session to try him. Talk of lynching followed, and a June 22 dispatch said two attempts to seize White had been foiled before daylight on June 21.

Word circulated on June 22 that the workhouse would be attacked at 10 p.m. after a gathering at Price's Corner, and thirty policemen sent there withdrew inside to help the guards. Attackers broke the doors with a battering ram of railroad ties, shots were exchanged, and Peter Smith, a boy in the crowd, was shot in the back. Told that White was in cell No. 13, they smashed the lever box, and Warden Meserve showed them how to open his cell so they would not take the wrong man.

Papers printed a confession White reportedly gave the mob, ending "You would not do this if I was a white man and did this." In a field near the scene of the crime, a rider on a white horse brought straw, and White was bound with rope and burned at a stake. When he broke loose he was struck with a fence rail and thrown back while the crowd cheered, and the next day thousands visited the site hunting relics.

The coroner's jury, with about five pounds of remains, found White burned to death by "a party or parties unknown." Arthur Corwell, the only person arrested, was dismissed by Magistrate Hollis on June 26 over the attorney general's objection. Peter Smith died June 24, and a coroner's jury named him Petro Allegretto, killed by "a person unknown."

Wilmington clergymen resolved their "sorrow, indignation and shame," though Rev. Robert A. Ellwood said people were "tired of the delays of the law." Armed disorder followed: on June 25 Black and white men clashed on Ninth Street, and William Cramer, a Black man, was shot by William Simms in an argument over the lynching. Rev. Montrose W. Thornton's call for a Black mass meeting was dropped after other ministers intervened, and Bishop M. B. Salter preached moderation.

In September Attorney General Ward questioned about twenty witnesses with little result, and the reputed leader, Baker, had left Wilmington. Chief Justice Lore told the grand jury that every wilful participant was a murderer, but it ignored the bill against eight persons, one juror saying, "The man got only what he deserved."

The Wilmington Evening Journal covered the case from the funeral to the grand jury and said the confession established "without doubt the guilt of the unfortunate negro." The wire narrative ran in the Washington Evening Star and other dailies, and follow-ups appeared in the New York Sun and Delaware and Maryland weeklies into September. The Smyrna Times disclaimed sympathy for "the rapist and murderer" but condemned "mob rule."

Black weeklies reprinted the same wire with its framing intact, the Wisconsin Weekly Advocate under "Sweet Young Girl Fiend's Victim" and the Afro-American stating that White "feloniously assaulted" Bishop. Their own comment was sharper: the Chicago Broad Ax mocked "four thousand Christians" and the police's "mighty poor effort," and the Savannah Tribune called the burning "another blot on the civilized world." In the fall the Advocate printed Lore's charge and then the headline "A VERY SMALL GRAND JURY," while the Cleveland Gazette ran "Lynchers Go Free."

Crowd estimates ran from 4,000 in the Afro-American to 5,000 to 6,000 in the Evening Star, with one wire report putting active participants at no more than 500. The warden said the guards fired over the crowd's heads, while the Afro-American reported that fire from inside brought down four of the mob.

reader.title: Lynching of George White
bases: A crowd of thousands broke into the New Castle County workhouse, took George White from his cell and burned him at a stake (A7, A32, A15).

White was taken from custody and burned to death by a crowd reported at 4,000 to 6,000, found by the coroner's jury to be 'parties unknown' (A7, A15, A32); the mob acted to punish his alleged assault and murder of Helen Bishop, and the papers tie it to impatience with 'the delays of the law' (A10, A54).
The local Evening Journal, the warden, the wire narrative in the Evening Star, a separate Afro-American special and the coroner's verdict agree on the break-in and burning (A4, A5, A7, A15, A32).

accounts.gist: The attack began at 10 and White was taken out at 12.05; guards fired over the crowd's heads while the mob fired at the windows; no Black person was in the building.

accounts.label: Wire narrative
accounts.gist: Leaders learned White was in cell 13, smashed the lever box, a leader shielded White from blows, and he was burned at a stake on Price's road after confessing.

accounts.label: Evening Journal local report
accounts.gist: A field was chosen near the scene of the crime; with a rope around his neck White was laid on an oil-soaked heap of straw and rails and thrown back when he tried to escape.

accounts.label: Afro-American special
accounts.gist: 4,000 men and boys led by a Virginian gathered at Price's Corner, broke four doors with railroad ties, and four of the mob fell under fire from inside before the guards gave way.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: White was burned to death by parties unknown between 10 p.m. June 22 and 4 a.m. June 23.

accounts.label: Reported confession
accounts.gist: Papers printed a confession White reportedly gave the mob, ending 'You would not do this if I was a white man'; the Evening Journal said he had also confessed in writing on Thursday.

accounts.label: Chicago Broad Ax
accounts.gist: The guards and police made 'a mighty poor effort' to protect White and the ringleaders wore women's dresses.

framing.detail: The Wilmington Evening Journal ran 'STORY OF BURNING' in detail and said the confession 'establishes without doubt the guilt of the unfortunate negro'.
The Evening Star and other dailies carried the long wire narrative, then headlined 'No Punishment Likely for Men Who Burned the Negro White'.
The Smyrna Times had 'no sympathy for the rapist and murderer' but condemned 'the supremacy of mob rule'.

The Wisconsin Weekly Advocate printed the wire under heads such as 'THEY CAN'T BE PUNISHED' and 'Sweet Young Girl Fiend's Victim'; the Afro-American headlined that 'Four Thousand Desperate Men ... Avenge the Murder of Miss Bishop'.
The Broad Ax mocked 'over four thousand Christians'; the Savannah Tribune called the burning 'another blot on the civilized world'; the Freeman and Colored American asked for punishment.
After the grand jury refused to indict, the Advocate wrote 'A VERY SMALL GRAND JURY' and the Cleveland Gazette headlined 'Lynchers Go Free'.
The Iowa Bystander printed Dr. Crum's condemnation of mob violence alongside a sermon by Rev. Dr. Bartlett defending those who 'burn the destroyer'.

record_check.dossier: Lynching on the night of June 22-23, 1903 (attack from 10 p.m. June 22; burned after midnight). June 21 is only the date of two failed earlier attempts.
New Castle County workhouse and a field on the road from Price's Corner to the Ferris Industrial School, outside Wilmington.

record_check.record: George White, Peter Smith, William White, Pietro Allegretto, G. J. Miller, Cornell, George Smith
record_check.dossier: George White only. Peter Smith and Petro Allegretto are one person, a boy in the attacking crowd shot at the workhouse; 'G. J. Miller' and 'George Smith' are garbles of White's name; Cornell (Arthur Corwell) was the accused lyncher; no 'William White' appears.
No hanging: a rope was thrown about his neck or wrapped round him and he was burned at a stake; the siege, shooting, beating (fence rail) and burning are reported.
A crowd of 4,000-6,000, a few hundred active, led by a man calling himself Baker; Arthur Corwell was arrested and dismissed; eight persons were named in a bill the grand jury ignored.
No Black person is reported injured in the lynching itself; the wounded were members of the attacking crowd (Peter Smith, 'the young Italian').
Two deaths in the attack: White, and Peter Smith (Allegretto), who died June 24. William Cramer's killing on June 25 is a separate later incident.

record_check.record: lynched early on June 23 ... no arrests reported
record_check.dossier: Arthur Corwell was arrested and dismissed; Attorney General Ward investigated and the grand jury ignored a bill against eight persons.
Charged with assaulting and killing Helen S. Bishop, 17.

info: Night of Monday, June 22-23, 1903: attack began about 10 p.m. June 22; White taken out after midnight; crowd dispersed about 2 a.m.; coroner fixed death between 10 p.m. June 22 and 4 a.m. June 23. Two earlier attempts failed before daylight on June 21.

New Castle County workhouse near Wilmington; burned in a field adjoining the road from Price's Corner to the Ferris Industrial School, near where Bishop was attacked. Price's Corner was four miles from Wilmington.
George White, a Black man ('a negro', 'a colored man'); also printed as 'George F. White', 'George Smith' and garbled as 'G. J. Miller'.

Charged with assaulting and killing Helen S. Bishop, 17, daughter of Rev. E. A. Bishop, attacked June 15 on her way home from school and dead the next day; papers printed a confession he reportedly gave the mob and a written confession reportedly made to workhouse authorities.

A crowd of men and boys from Wilmington and nearby towns, organized in advance; leader called himself 'Baker' and said he was from Virginia; a man on a white horse, said to be from Kentucky, brought straw. The warden said no Black person was in the building.
No one was indicted; the reputed leader Baker had left Wilmington.
